REMOVAL OF A CORPORATE OFFICER — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE
This Information Sheet describes California Corporations Code section 312 — the statutory provisions governing which officers a California corporation must have, how those officers are chosen, and the board of directors' statutory authority over an officer's continued service in office. It is prepared with reference to Jordan Alex Lee's service as President of Acme, Inc. This Information Sheet is a general reference describing what section 312 provides; it does not evaluate, and is not evidence of, whether removing Jordan Alex Lee from the office of President would be proper under any specific circumstances, whether such a removal would breach any contract of employment, or what Acme, Inc.'s board of directors should do. Those are fact-specific questions this Information Sheet does not answer. This document is a companion to, and does not duplicate, this project's existing Corporate Bylaws document, whose officers clause states only a general default (that officers are chosen by the board and serve at the board's discretion) without quoting the statutory text or addressing the statute's rules on required offices, dual office-holding, resignation, or the officer's contract rights that this document addresses in depth.

THE OFFICERS A CALIFORNIA CORPORATION MUST HAVE
California law requires every California corporation to have certain officers: (1) a chairperson of the board — who may instead, or in addition, be given the title of president — (2) a secretary, and (3) a chief financial officer, along with any other officers with titles and duties stated in the bylaws or determined by the board that are necessary to enable the corporation to sign instruments and share certificates. Unless the articles or bylaws provide otherwise, the president (or, if there is no president, the chairperson of the board) is by default the corporation's general manager and chief executive officer. This clause states which offices the statute requires and who functions as chief executive officer by default; it does not state which of Acme, Inc.'s existing offices satisfy each statutory category, and it does not evaluate whether Acme, Inc.'s articles or bylaws have departed from these statutory defaults.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "A corporation shall have (1) a chairperson of the board, who may be given the title of chair of the board, chairperson of the board, chairperson, or a president or both, (2) a secretary, (3) a chief financial officer, and (4) such other officers with such titles and duties as shall be stated in the bylaws or determined by the board and as may be necessary to enable it to sign instruments and share certificates."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 312(a) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, required corporate officers (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=312.)
  "The president, or if there is no president the chairperson of the board, is the general manager and chief executive officer of the corporation, unless otherwise provided in the articles or bylaws."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 312(a) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, default chief executive officer (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=312.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes two sentences from a single subdivision (subdivision (a)) of Corporations Code section 312; the two quotations are not independent sources of one another. It does not address subdivision (b) of the same section, which governs how officers are chosen and removed and an officer's right to resign — covered in separate clauses of this document using the same statute. This clause does not identify which title, if any, an officer's stated office corresponds to under the statute's own categories.

HOLDING MORE THAN ONE OFFICE
California law permits any number of corporate offices to be held by the same person, unless a corporation's articles of incorporation or bylaws provide otherwise. This clause states the default statutory rule; it does not determine whether Acme, Inc.'s own articles or bylaws restrict Jordan Alex Lee or any other individual from holding more than one office at the same time.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Any number of offices may be held by the same person unless the articles or bylaws provide otherwise."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 312(a) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, one person holding multiple offices (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=312.)
  Known gap: This is the same subdivision of Corporations Code section 312 (subdivision (a)) quoted in the preceding clause of this document — not an independent source corroborating it. The statute does not state whether the corporation's minimum required officer positions (described in the preceding clause) may all be satisfied by a single office-holder in every circumstance; this clause states only the general dual-office-holding default.

HOW OFFICERS ARE CHOSEN AND THE BOARD'S AUTHORITY OVER THEIR CONTINUED SERVICE
Under California law, unless a corporation's articles or bylaws provide otherwise, a corporation's officers are chosen by the board of directors, and an officer serves at the pleasure of the board. This means the board holds the statutory power to end an officer's service in that office, and the statute does not condition that power on the board having any particular reason for doing so. The statute expressly makes this board authority subject to "the rights, if any, of an officer under any contract of employment" — meaning the statute itself preserves whatever separate contractual rights an officer may have, without stating what those rights are or whether any specific contract creates them. This clause states the statutory default itself; it does not state whether Acme, Inc.'s articles or bylaws have altered this default, whether Jordan Alex Lee has an employment contract, or what rights any such contract might create.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Except as otherwise provided by the articles or bylaws, officers shall be chosen by the board and serve at the pleasure of the board, subject to the rights, if any, of an officer under any contract of employment."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 312(b) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, selection of officers and the board's authority over an officer's continued service (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=312.)
  Known gap: This is subdivision (b) of Corporations Code section 312, the same statutory subdivision quoted in the following clause of this document (which addresses an officer's own right to resign) — not an independent source corroborating it. The statute uses the phrase "serve at the pleasure of the board"; the quoted text does not itself contain the phrase "with or without cause," and this clause does not represent that it does. The statute states that this board authority is subject to an officer's contract rights, if any, but does not itself define what a contract of employment must contain to create such rights, and does not state whether removing a specific officer without cause would constitute a breach of any specific contract — those are fact-specific and contract-specific questions this clause does not answer.

AN OFFICER'S RIGHT TO RESIGN
California law also gives an officer the separate, reciprocal right to resign from office at any time, on written notice to the corporation. The statute states that a resignation is without prejudice to any rights the corporation may separately have under a contract to which the resigning officer is a party. This clause states the statutory resignation right and the statute's preservation of the corporation's own contract rights; it does not state whether Acme, Inc. has a contract with Jordan Alex Lee or what rights, if any, that contract would preserve.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Any officer may resign at any time upon written notice to the corporation without prejudice to the rights, if any, of the corporation under any contract to which the officer is a party."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 312(b) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, an officer's right to resign (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=312.)
  Known gap: This is the same subdivision of Corporations Code section 312 (subdivision (b)) quoted in the preceding clause of this document — not an independent source. The statute does not specify a notice period, form, or delivery method for an officer's resignation beyond stating that notice must be in writing and given to the corporation.

HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM AT-WILL EMPLOYEE STATUS
Corporations Code section 312 and its "serve at the pleasure of the board" rule govern the corporate-law validity of removing a person from a corporate office — a title and role created by the corporation's own governance structure. That is a separate body of law from the common default rule for a rank-and-file employee's job, found in Labor Code section 2922, which provides that an employment relationship with no specified term may be terminated at the will of either party on notice to the other. An individual can simultaneously hold a corporate office covered by section 312 and be an employee of the corporation covered by section 2922 (or by a separate employment contract); the two statutes address two different legal relationships — the office, and the employment — and removal from one does not by itself state what happens to the other. This clause states that these are separate statutes governing separate relationships; it does not state whether Jordan Alex Lee's relationship with Acme, Inc. includes an employment relationship distinct from the office of President, or what would happen to any such employment relationship if Jordan Alex Lee were removed from office.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Except as otherwise provided by the articles or bylaws, officers shall be chosen by the board and serve at the pleasure of the board, subject to the rights, if any, of an officer under any contract of employment."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 312(b) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, the board's authority over a corporate office (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=312.)
  "An employment, having no specified term, may be terminated at the will of either party on notice to the other."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 2922 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, default at-will rule for an employment relationship (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2922.)
  Known gap: Corporations Code section 312 and Labor Code section 2922 are independently numbered statutes in different codes, not subsections of the same section — genuinely independent sources, unlike the other citation pairs in this document. This clause states only that these are distinct legal relationships governed by distinct statutes; it does not describe the statutory and common-law exceptions to at-will employment under California law (such as express or implied contract terms, or public-policy limits), which this project's other documents cover separately, and it does not state whether any specific facts would place a given officer's situation within such an exception.

RECORD AND CERTIFICATION
This record concerns the office of President, held by Jordan Alex Lee at Acme, Inc. It certifies only that the description of California Corporations Code section 312 in this Information Sheet reflects the statutory text as in effect on the date below, and that this Information Sheet is a general informational reference regarding Jordan Alex Lee's service as President of Acme, Inc. — not legal advice about, and not a record of any determination, whether removing Jordan Alex Lee from that office is proper, whether such a removal would breach any contract, or what Acme, Inc.'s board of directors has decided or should decide.

Executed on September 1, 2026 at Oakland, California.

Signature of Jordan T. Reyes: _________________________
